Title: Radiative Stabilization of the Indenyl Cation: Recurrent Fluorescence in a Closed-Shell Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon
Text:
Radiative Stabilization of the Indenyl Cation: Recurrent Fluorescence in a Closed-Shell
Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon
James N. Bull ,1,2,* Arun Subramani ,3 Chang Liu ,4 Samuel J. P. Marlton ,4 Eleanor K. Ashworth ,1
Henrik Cederquist ,3 Henning Zettergren ,3 and Mark H. Stockett

Several small polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) with closed-shell electronic structure have been
identified in the cold, dark environment Taurus Molecular Cloud 1. We measure efficient radiative cooling
through the combination of recurrent fluorescence (RF) and IR emission in the closed-shell indenyl cation
(C9Hþ
7 ), finding good agreement with a master equation model including molecular dynamics trajectories
to describe internal-energy-dependent properties for RF. We find that C9Hþ

DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.228002
The discovery of small polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon
(PAH) molecules in interstellar clouds through radio
astronomy [1–7] and observations of infrared (IR) emission
bands from PAHs with unprecedented sensitivity by the
James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) [8–10] is opening up
a new era for laboratory investigations of PAH unimolec-
ular dynamics. The general consensus is that PAHs are
widespread in space [11], with data from the Spitzer Space
Telescope and JWST supporting that up to 20% of Galactic
carbon is present as PAHs [8,10,12–14]. To date, fewer than
ten specific PAH-based molecules have been discovered in
space. In all cases, identifications were made in Taurus
Molecular Cloud 1 (TMC-1) through the comparison of
observed rotational lines with spectra recorded in the
laboratory [2–5]. However, the observed abundances of
these PAHs (1-cyanonaphthalene, 2-cyanonaphthalene,
indene, 2-cyanoindene, 1=5-cyanoacenaphthylene, and
isomers of cyanopyrene) are orders of magnitude higher
than astrophysical models predict, implying that the effi-
ciencies of destruction channels are overestimated, and/or
that the efficiencies of molecular formation and stabiliza-
tion processes are underestimated.
In the cold molecular cloud where these specific PAHs
were discovered, molecules are mostly shielded from the
harsh interstellar radiation field [15]. The main destruction
mechanisms included in astrochemical models are thermal
(≈10 K) collisions with atomic and molecular cations
[1,2,16–19]. These models do not consider if the resulting
PAH cations may be reneutralized through electron-ion
recombination or by mutual neutralization in collisions
with anions, in addition to not including efficient (barrier-
less) ion-molecule bottom-up formation mechanisms, with
recombination leading to the observed neutral PAHs [1,2].
All of these reactions may generate neutral PAHs with
internal energies similar to or in excess of their respective
dissociation thresholds. It is therefore necessary to under-
stand how energized closed-shell PAHs may stabilize
through radiative cooling.
In a step toward investigating the radiative cooling
processes contributing to PAH life cycles, laboratory studies
on isolated open-shell (radical cation) PAHs using electro-
static ion-beam storage devices [20–25]—including under
“molecular cloud in a box” conditions (P ≈10−14 mbar,
T ≈13 K) at the DESIREE infrastructure [26,27]—have
shown that recurrent fluorescence (RF), or Poincar´e fluo-
rescence [28,29], plays a crucial role. Similar experiments
have shown that RF dominates the cooling of odd-electron
carbon chain anions and fullerene ions [29–34]. However,
while ionized PAHs are expected to exist in bright or star-
forming regions of space [35], it is their neutral (closed-shell)
forms that have been observed in dark interstellar clouds
[2–4]. Closed-shell PAHs typically have different electronic
structure than their open-shell cations [36,37]. In particular,

more) totheir first few electronicallyexcitedstates;therefore,
from results on open-shell PAH cations, one cannot infer
directly that RF processes will be similarly active for closed-
shell PAHs. From the perspective of laboratory experiments,
it is not possible to store neutral PAHs, or investigate
radiative cooling dynamics, over timescales relevant for
determining
their
decay
properties
(microseconds
to
minutes). Thus, it is necessary to find other ways to
investigate the balance between radiative stabilization and
decay (fragmentation) of internally hot, closed-shell PAHs.
Here, we present experimental and theoretical results on
highly efficient radiative cooling of the indenyl cation
[½In-Hþ; C9Hþ
7 , Fig. 1(a)]. This ion has a closed-shell
electronic structure and transition probabilities similar to
neutral PAHs with 20 or more carbon atoms (see the
Supplemental Material [38]). In TMC-1, ½In-Hþ may be
formed in ionizing collisions between indene and atomic
cations, which is assumed to be the major destruction
pathway for PAHs there [1]. Outside of cold molecular
clouds, ½In-Hþ may form with near unit quantum yield
following the dissociative ionization of indene (C9H8) by
hν ¼ 13.6 eV (H-ionization) radiation [68]. Importantly, to
date, indene is the only pure PAH that has been observed
in TMC-1 or in space. Therefore, information on the
stabilities and reactivities of its precursors as well as those
of its fragments, such as C9Hþ
7 , is crucial for estimates of
abundances [2].
The present experiments were performed at the electro-
static ion-beam storage ring DESIREE [26,27], shown in
Fig. 1(b). There, we monitored the generation of neutral
particles following thermal activation of the stored ions in a
8.6 m circumference storage ring (Supplemental Material
[38]). Cryogenic cooling of the storage ring to T ≈13 K
gives a residual gas density of ≈104 particles=cm3 (mostly
H2) [27], allowing ions to be stored in a nearly collision-free
environment for hours [69]. For ensembles of internally
excited C9Hþ
7 , we measured the RðtÞ of neutral particles
(dissociation products) leaving the ensemble and ring as a
function of the time t after injection. At longer times, RðtÞ is

Schematic illustrations of RðtÞ data under different cooling
scenarios are given in the Supplemental Material [38]. The
measured RðtÞ distribution is shown in Fig. 1(c), with the
dissociation signal dominated by the generation of C2H2,
giving m=z ¼ 89 as the cyclopentadienyl acetylene cation
and benzocyclopropyl cation isomers in a 2∶1 ratio as
confirmed through ion mobility spectrometry—see the
Supplemental Material [38]—when vibrational energies
are within a few electronvolts of the dissociation threshold.
Loss of C4H2 and C4H4 becomes important at higher
vibrational energies beyond the range considered in this
work (Table S2). RðtÞ is well-described by the expression
RðtÞ ¼ r0t−αe−kct;

where r0 is the initial signal amplitude and kc is a character-
istic rate. Parameter k−1
c
is the characteristic time at which
dissociation is quenched by radiative emission. Equation (1)
assumes that the count rate at short time follows a power law,
RðtÞ ∝t−α [70], because of the broad vibrational energy
distribution, gðE; tÞ, and the rapid variation of the dissoci-
ation rate coefficient, kdðEÞ, with the internal excitation
energy, E [71]. A fit of Eq. (1) to our RðtÞ data [the black
curve in Fig. 1(c)] returned kc ¼ 508  5 s−1 and α ¼
0.787  0.005, where kc is larger than for radical cations
of naphthalene (460  5 s−1) [25], 1-cyanonaphthalene
(300  20 s−1) [23], or the kc values for larger PAHs such
as anthracene, tetracene, or perylene [24,72,73]. Importantly,
photons from RF processes have been directly observed for
naphthalene and anthracene cations [22,74], highlighting
that RF is a necessary factor for the cooling dynamics in PAH
radical cations with large kc values. Typically, kc for systems
with only IR cooling are ∼100 s−1 [75]. We conclude that
radiative cooling is particularly efficient in ½In-Hþ.
While a large value of kc implies efficient radiative
cooling, it does not yield any information on the detailed
relaxation mechanisms. We use experimental parameters to
convert the RðtÞ data to absolute rates per molecule, ΓðtÞ, as
shown in Fig. 1(d) (see also the Supplemental Material
[38]). We model the rates, shown in Fig. 2, for dissociation
(kd) using RRKM theory, RF emission (kRF) via internal-
energy-dependent geometries and associated transition
energies and oscillator strengths obtained from ab initio
molecular dynamics (AIMD) trajectories, and IR emission
(kIR)
using
a
simple
harmonic
cascade
framework
[23,25,76]. These three processes were combined in a
coupled master equation to model ΓðtÞ [black trace in
Fig. 1(d)]. The model results are in good agreement with
the experimental data.
A key outcome from the modeling is that if RF is
excluded, we arrive at the dashed curve in Fig. 1(d), which
substantially overestimates the dissociation rate. Moreover,
the use of static oscillator strengths at the molecular
equilibrium geometry (i.e., assuming T ¼ 0 K) for RF
gave an observed dissociation curve close to the “no RF”
case, showing that internal-energy-dependent (i.e., temper-
ature-dependent) effects leading to geometric distortions,
which were incorporated here using AIMD trajectories, are
critical for a realistic description of the RF process. Indeed,
while earlier studies on open-shell PAH cations have
suggested that kRF may be significantly underestimated
by static calculations of kRF and sought to include
Herzberg-Teller coupling [77] at the equilibrium geometry
to more robustly describe oscillator strengths [23,25], the
use of AIMD trajectories to determine internal-energy-
dependent transition energies and probabilities provides a
decisive step in describing RF. The present AIMD trajec-
tory strategy is readily applied to other open- and closed-
shell PAHs.
Taking the kRF and kd rates from Fig. 2, the modeled
survival probability for ½In-Hþ as a function of vibrational
energy is shown in the inset in Fig. 1(d), returning the
critical vibrational energy Ec ¼ 5.85 eV, above which the
ions are more likely to be destroyed (fragmented), and
below which they are more likely to be stabilized through

radiative emission. Significantly, Ec is ≈2 eV higher than
the lowest bond dissociation energy (BDE), which we
calculated here to be 3.74 eV (see the Supplemental
Material [38]). This clearly demonstrates the importance
of RF for the stabilization of the closed-shell PAH
cation ½In-Hþ.
We now consider how the radiative cooling dynamics
observed for ½In-Hþ relate to neutral PAHs that may be
present in dark molecular clouds, which, like ½In-Hþ, have
closed-shell electronic structures. Based on the close
agreement found between theory and experiment for the
cooling of ½In-Hþ, and established trends in key molecular
properties of PAHs with increasing size, predications on the
rates for dissociation, IR emission, and RF for other PAHs
are possible. First, dissociation rates within an RRKM
framework decrease with increasing PAH size (i.e., heat
capacity) because, while exceptions will exist, H-loss
dissociation energies show little variation across PAHs
containing 10–24 carbon atoms [78,79], with astrochemical
models often assuming values of 4.1–4.6 eV [80,81].
Similarly, because IR emission rates are usually dominated
by a few bright modes that are common across PAHs as a
class, the total IR emission rate slowly decreases with
increasing size and heat capacity [35]. On the other hand,
while the first electronic transition energies of closed-shell
PAHs have some dependence on the chemical structure, the
overall trend is that the corresponding excitation energies
decrease with increasing PAH size [82], which favors
stabilization through RF and counteracts the effect of
increasing heat capacity. For example, transition energies
in acenes containing 10 to 20 carbon atoms, including
nonlinear, 2D, and structural isomers, systematically
decrease from ≈3 to 1.5 eV [37,83–85], approaching that
of ½In-Hþ at 1.2 eV (S1), but also have oscillator strengths
that are larger than ½In-Hþ by at least an order of
magnitude. This indicates that RF will tend to become
more important with increasing PAH size; however, com-
putational studies on a range of neutral PAHs using our (or
a similar) modeling framework are desirable to more
precisely quantify the degree to which these trends scale.
This work has demonstrated efficient radiative cooling in
a small, closed-shell PAH molecule, in which RF plays a
dominant role in quenching dissociation for internal ener-
gies up to Ec ¼ 5.85 eV. Our target system, C9Hþ
7 , is of
similar size to the smallest neutral, closed-shell PAHs
observed in TMC-1 through radio astronomy, suggesting
that other similarly sized, closed-shell PAHs also may have
efficient cooling dynamics. The enhanced survivability of
energized neutral PAHs with efficient RF cooling means
that the abundance of small, closed-shell PAHs (i.e., the
building blocks in bottom-up growth astrochemistry)
inherited from earlier stages of molecular cloud formation
may be higher than expected [1–7]. Ultimately, this work
demonstrates that RF must be considered in astrophysical
molecular abundance models in order to reliably predict
contributions to aromatic infrared bands (AIBs) and other
IR observations for closed-shell PAHs [11,86], and that the
RF influence will become gradually more important for
larger PAHs. The exceptionally good agreement found here
for the measured dissociation rate between experiment and
theory for a prototype closed-shell PAH means that our
cooling model, combining internal-energy-dependent tran-
sition energies and oscillator strengths for describing RF,
can be applied to predict the radiative cooling rates of other
closed-shell PAH molecules.
